The sign also includes the logo for Tennis Australia and the slogan "The Power of Play." The man appears to be at an event related to tennis coaching, as indicated by the context provided by the sign.

Coaches, our next presenter is Frank Gianparlo, the Tennis Pro Author and Vice-Chair of the USTA SCTA Coach Commission. Frank is an award-winning coach and author of influential books like the Tennis Parents Bible and Championship Tennis. With a career spanning over 30 years, Frank has developed 100 national champions. In his session, Beyond Technique, Frank will share his innovative methods for advancing play performance through holistic coaching. Welcome Frank. My name is from Southern California, I'm Frank Gianparlo and I've been doing this stuff for about 40 years so I'm going to give you some of my best tips, 20 tips in 20 minutes. We're going to go beyond teaching technique so let's go for it. Okay number one, it's our job to teach our athletes that they have three different performances. So one is the point, that's the three to five seconds of hitting and running and I would call that the hardware of an athlete. The second performance is of course, you know, in between points, right? And that's the software, that's the mental and emotional skills. The third performance is when they sit down for the 90 second changeover and they have a job to do there as well. So first performance, actually the tennis identity of that athlete and their top patterns of play, we're trying to get them to expose that. The second performance in between points is basically they're resetting routines, right?

How can they get over drama, there's going to be drama, there's going to be hardship in every match and the best athletes are prepared with solutions already. The third performance when they sit down, of course, they have internal and external routines and it's our job to teach that. Internal might be the thinking external, the outer. So external might be make sure they're sitting, deep breathing, lowering their heart rate, right? That calming down, make sure they're hydrating, of course, towel off. The internal, that might be a little bit different, that might be just thinking two games back and two games forward. So with my athletes here in California and around the country, we teach them that think two games back, did I hold or did I break? Why or why not? How did I hold? Okay, if I just take good kick serves into the backhand and got short balls that I held easy, don't change it. Did I break the other dudes? That's what we see in Southern California, dudes. Did we break the other dudes serve? Why or why not? I didn't hit two returns in the net. Okay, so I got to stand two big steps farther back, I'm going to adjust and go more high and heavy, deep down the middle in the returns. So they get a drink, they hydrate and before they run back out, they're going to rehearse that in their mind. How do I hold? How do I break? All right, three performances that you're teaching. Number two, we want to make sure that we're teaching them to have goal setting and this

is performance goals, not outcome goals. Of course, everybody wants the outcome, but they don't have the systems in place to make the outcome work. So performance goals might be set achievable, realistic goals like simply 60% first serves in or any short balls move inside the court and flatten it out. When you're on defense, hit more high and heavy. That would be three basic performance goals. And it's our job to teach the parent that as well because remember when the child goes out, especially here in the States, when the child goes out to play tournaments, they're going with the parent, they're not going with their primary coach. And so really, we don't really know what's going on as coaches, correct? The parents are the primary coach, they're like, we would call it the weekend coach. So we want to teach them as well. When they're presetting these performance goals like the week before the tournament, make sure they're doing periodization training. So they're adding anything new, like a new gym workout the day before a tournament. They're not trying to change strokes before a tournament, they're doing what's comfortable. And be careful. Here's one of the mistakes I made a couple of years ago. I took a group of kids to the All You Can Eat Indian Buffet at the tournament site and they all lost after that and it was kind of my fault because, I mean, the food was great, let me tell you.

Yeah, maybe they should be eating things that are comfortable. So that's big, that type of periodization training. All right, number three, teach your athletes that visualization is very, very important. This is mental rehearsal and I have a book out and you're going to receive it. It's one of the free books you're going to get. It's called Neuropriming for Peak Performance. And it's basically teaching the athlete their solutions to their physical, their strokes, their mental, their strategy, tactics, how to beat different styles of people, for example. And emotional, how to handle choking, panicking, tanking. So what they do is they take these different types of scripts and you can do this with your athletes. It's very meaningful. But they write these down, they write the solutions down, how they're going to handle these problems. And then they write it down and they record it onto their cell phone, just like I'm recording this on my cell phone. And then they listen to their recordings at night as they're falling asleep, as their subconscious mind awakes, they're listening to their audio tapes of solutions. And before matches, instead of hanging out with their friends, have them sit in the car a little bit and listen to their audio tapes of solutions, okay? So visualization is pretty big. Number four, nutrition and hydration. I'm going to change the name of this athlete to protect the guilty, but I had a student

in Florida. He was 80 in their section and he became number one in about eight months. He was number one. One of the big keys we had to do is change his nutrition and hydration. So this athlete, 11-year-old Matthew, he was very hyper, he had a lot of energy, high metabolism. He would play tennis trained for five or six hours a day. And on average, especially in Florida, in that type of heat, they're burning about a thousand calories a day. So let's say he's burning 5,000 calories a day, he would be eating 1,500 calories a day. And his dad would be asking, why is my son so skinny and frail? He plays tennis all day, why is he so skinny? And that's the reason why. We have to kind of make sure that they're eating a little bit more calories than they're actually burning, right? And number five, this is kind of the dynamic warm-up that we want to make sure you're teaching your athlete and the parents, right? But the athlete has to morph into a warrior. It's a character. It's like they're an actor going to a TV show, a TV shoot in Hollywood. They have to morph into character, okay? So that's really important. Obviously, they have to warm up their body, short-run, do their dynamic stretches, of course, and make sure they have a band routine where they're doing their stretch bands and they're building their upper body, shoulders, and core, because you know core is paid. So make sure they're doing that before matches.

And again, remind them that it's in their best interest to stay away from hanging out with their friends before the match. Especially when they hang out with their friends, their friends are all talking about outcome goals and outcome scenarios, and you want your athlete to stay in the performance goal realm, right? Okay, so you got five right there, and we're going to keep going. All right, let's continue with this preparing for pressure type of topic. Number six, when the athletes are warming up, ask them to warm up their primary and secondary strokes. And so here's a painter's analogy. An intermediate painter would just have a primary strip of basic colors. There'd be a primary strip of paint of black, brown, blue, green, red, yellow, basic colors. Now they would paint with that, and they would always get just average paintings. Now the top painters know that it's not just primary colors, but secondary colors. So they don't have a green. They have six, seven versions of green on their palette. And now their paintings are more lifelike and real, they're high level paintings. And that's what we want from our athletes. So your athlete doesn't have a forehand. They have six different forehands. They have drive, height and heavy, short angles, slices, drop shots, lobs, six, of course if they have six forehands, they have six backhands, same six. And three serves, flat kick, slice, they're warming up the whole tool belt, volleys.

Not just standing at the net, coiling and doing primary punch volleys, but we're warming up swing volleys, drop volleys, transition volleys. That's important. So make sure that your athletes are warming up their secondary strokes, because you know and I know, parents might not know, but the athlete needs the secondary strokes. They might actually get into a tiebreaker and need a swing volley or a topspin lob over the opponent's head to win the tiebreaker. And if they're not warmed up and ready to go, if they're kind of rusty, you know they're in trouble. So warm those up to a little bit before matches. Number seven on your list, teach your athletes to invite the flow state. And that's what's playing in their subconscious mind. So think about it like this and you can teach your athletes that they have their conscious mind. This is their editing and judgmental mind. That's great in practice when they're fixing strokes, the biomechanics and the follow-throughs and things like that. They want to work on that, right? And they want to be in their conscious editing mind. In a match, they want to be in their subconscious mind. They want to be more free flowing, right? You don't want athletes to destroy their subconscious mind because that's where playing in the zone comes from. They destroy it by being too judgmental, too critical, too over analytical. Some athletes really just overanalyze everything and they kill themselves in pressure.

So that's number seven. Number eight, heart rate monitoring. This is something I've been doing for a couple of years now and I'll give you a real example. An athlete, I have Josh, he wears an eye watch or you can have your athletes wear a Fitbit which are very inexpensive. So when Josh is playing, when his heart rate is around 110, it's too low, 110 beats per minute. It's too low. He has to pay attention to that, pump himself up, do some shadow swings, get his energy up a little bit. Now when his heart rate is 200, 210, when it's too high, he's freaking out. Josh is in a panic mode and when he's panicking, he's not problem solving. He's not thinking because I'm making good decisions. And very important though, being in the zone is playing at a good heart rate. So usually it's around 150 to 170 beats per minute, but every athlete's a little bit different. But if you can get them to understand their heart rate, that's big. I think that's why Raphael Nadal, after changeovers, his heart rate is lower. He would get up and he would sprint back out to the baseline to get his heart rate up and to his peak performance level. So try that with a Fitbit, try it with an eye watch. And coaches, if you have a wife like mine that's bugging you to get your 10,000 steps in every day, here's a good tip. Take your Fitbit, put it around your dog's collar, have them go outside and run around in the yard for a while.

Then when he comes in, you got the Fitbit, it says 10,000 feet steps and you're good. So there's that. Number nine, it's really important that you want to remind your athletes that expectations and pre-match speculations, they're only illusions. It's not real. This happens very often. So like one of my gals, Ava, she's playing a girl Zoe in the tournament coming up. She goes, well, you know, my friend Kelly beat Zoe easy and I beat Kelly two and two. So I'm going to probably win that round either easy, I'm going to be in the second round of the tournament, then I'm going to play this person, then that person. And the speculation really goes nuts, right? So what happens is Ava's in the tournament, Ava's now playing Zoe. She doesn't handle that style of play that well. Now she's in tiebreakers and she's freaking out mad because she's speculated that she would win easy because her friend Kelly did. So manage these expectations, speculations. I think it's very important. Let's go number 10, decision-making under pressure. This is so important, but we all hear it, every coach hears it. The parents say, you know, my kid is so good in practice, but they stink in a match and I don't know why, what gives, why? Well, remember competitive tennis is not a cooperative game of catch back and forth. It's a violent game of keep away. So we have to have our athletes practice in the manner they're expected to perform.

If they're out there just rallying and playing catch and hitting it back to the coach and they look terrific in practice, that's great, but that's not going to really help as much. So practice running their plays and patterns, and these are like keep away plays, right? And it's really important with biomechanics that kids practice changing incoming angles, incident reflected angles. They have to change, they have to practice changing, not just hitting it back to a person, but how to hit it away from a person. So we want to make sure that they're practicing that under pressure and make sure they're playing a lot of practice matches, because that's where decision making and problem solving comes into play. Kids that are really good at problem solving, they're the ones that win the tight matches. All right, we're moving on. Number 11 in this little group of 20, we want to make sure the athletes and the parents understand what amygdala hijack is, and they have to manage that. So another name for that is the emotional hijack. And we've all seen it, athletes miss a few shots, they're getting into some drama, they start to freak out, and they get so upset they can't play anymore. And sometimes they win the whole first, you know, first at 6-2, they're up 4-1, now they start thinking about the outcome too much, who are they going to play next, which my ranking going to go to, what are my friends going to say, they start making mistakes,

they're trying to get upset, and they get emotionally hijacked. Now once that happens, they're done, they can't problem solve anymore, they can't find their correct motor programs for their strokes. And so managing this kind of emotional hijack is very important. I try to get the kids to use what I would call the balloon analogy. So I have them pretend that right above their head, there's a stressed balloon, and when they miss a shot, they're blowing air into the balloon, they're inflating it, right? Inflating. They miss a couple more shots, and they're inflating it more and more and more. If they keep on doing that without resetting, without deflating the balloon, it pops. And once it pops, they are done. So when they make mistakes, they have to go to the back fence, reset a little bit, de-stress, take the air out of the stressed balloon, if they keep on taking the air out of it, it won't pop. All right, number 12. I know what you're thinking, man, this, either you're thinking, this guy's crazy, or this is really good stuff. I don't know, you have to let me know. Number 12, oxygen regulation. And a junior, Joey, who was 10 from Las Vegas, he described it like this, he goes, man, it's just like the dolphins in the ocean. They can swim like 300, 400 miles overnight, this little 10-year-old kid told me. But they have to go up and breathe, go down and kick, kick, kick, kick, kick, kick, kick,

go up and breathe, go down and kick, go up and breathe, and it's a routine, and it's oxygen. Well, that's important. That's like your athletes doing the in-between-point routines where they're breathing. Why? It's going to enhance endurance, it's going to increase energy, it's going to improve their mental focus, it's going to reduce this lactic acid buildup, which kind of delays the muscle recovery. And to me, it supports not only the muscles, but the lungs and the brain. So oxygen, it's more important than you think. And you know, a lot of kids say, man, you don't need to teach me how to breathe. I can breathe. I don't have to think about breathing. But actually, they do in a match. That's important. 13 is managing these software skills. So let's go into that a little bit deeper right now. Look at your athletes the same way you look at a computer. There's hardware and there's software, and it has to flow seamlessly together in a match. So their hardware is their strokes, the tool belt of all their strokes, and their athleticism, right? This is speed, agility, stamina, endurance. That's all hardware. And that's what most coaches teach. Now the software is probably even more important, in my opinion, at the higher levels. Once you start competing, the software is mental and emotional. Mental skills are thinking skills, like my tennis identity, my strategy, my tactics, my opponent awareness.

Emotional skills might be things like managing performance anxieties, like fear, nervousness, choking, panicking, that type of thing. So hardware, software. Let's talk for a second about this thinking beyond fundamentals, I think it's important. Here's a couple of software skills that you could teach the athletes and the parents. In a match, in between points, they have to know self-awareness. What am I doing right or wrong, good or bad? What's working? What's not? They have to know opponent awareness. What is the opponent doing over there, good or bad, right or wrong? What do they like, dislike? It's opponent awareness. Score management. Score management is big. A lot of times, as coaches, we say, hey, man, this is a big point. This is a game point. So pay attention. Well, not all game points are the same. There are positive and negative game points. Positive game point is when your athlete is up, like 40, 15, they should step inside the court more, be a little more bold. When your athlete is in a negative game point, that's when they have 15, the opponent has It's a very different situation. And when they're in a negative game point, it's probably in their best interest to use bigger margins, height over the net, two or three feet inside the lines, that's big. Score management, that's important. So now, momentum management, that's big. Focus management, that's huge, because we know that that's the basis of concentration.

That's the basis of a person playing in there, like subconscious mind, is their focus. And then intensity management. These are things probably that the US college coaches talk about more than just fundamental stroke. They talk about managing these software skills. All right, we're at 14, we're rocking right now, so present moment awareness. It's our job to ask the athletes to pay attention to where their focus, where their thoughts are. Sometimes they're in a match and they're not in the present moment awareness, which is what am I doing right now? Can I win this point? How am I going to win this next point right now? Present moment. Past is maybe when they're frustrated. Usually when a kid is frustrated, an adult athlete is frustrated, they're thinking about the past. That could be an easy mistake they made, that could be a bad line call, thinking about the past. Thinking about the past too much, catastrophic. Who's going to win? Who's going to lose? What are my parents going to say? You know the whole deal about future thoughts. So present moment awareness, that's big. And number 15 on the list, probably my favorite is positive self-coaching. It's our job to teach the athletes how to teach themselves. And so here's something I did on a personal note with my daughter when she was younger. She was 10, she was a great soccer player, she decided to start to play tennis. I didn't want her to play tennis because I was already a high-performance coach for

about 15 years before she even started. Well, Sarah went kind of serious into tennis and she went from being more of an intermediate beginner player when she started because she was a good athlete. She was number one in the nation and then she played the U.S. Open by a lot of athletes. She was number one in the nation and then she played the U.S. Open by 15 years old. So she had a really good run, she played at USC after that, terrific. But here's what we did, the co-pilot game. So whenever we would travel to tournaments, this is driving to a tournament or flying, she would have to be in charge even at 10 years old of the navigational system. So I would have her do this. She would have to find the airport, she'd have to find parking. She would tell me how to get on the bus and go to the terminal. She would be in charge of finding the American Airlines counter. She's in charge of getting through TSA security. She's in charge of finding her gate. She's in charge of finding our seat on the plane. When we land, she's in charge of finding baggage claim at the airport. She's in charge of finding the rental car. And then she's in charge of finding the hotel or the tournament site. Now when she does that, guess what she's doing? She's practicing problem solving. The kids that play great in tournaments usually are really solid problem solvers. So that's part of this on a positive side of coaching.

And let me even add a little bit of a trick. This is big, I think. Teach your parents of athletes, and you can do it yourself, to ask versus telling the student what to do. Do not tell them what to do. Ask them, what do they think they should do? How do they think they should find the solution? So when you tell them there's resistance, right, and they feel like disrespected and they give little effort because you're telling them what to do. When you're asking them, they feel respected, right? They take ownership in it. And it helps them boost their confidence level when you believe in them. So don't tell them what to do. Ask them what to do. Okay. Anyway, hope you guys are enjoying this stuff. And let's go. 16 are coming down to the wire here. So we want to teach your athletes that they have to rebound from hardship. We have to teach them how to do that and why it's so important. So I'm going to give you a little story. It's a rattlesnake analogy. So if a rattlesnake bites you, is it the little bite that kills you or the venom coursing through your veins for the next 10 hours? So venom, right? Now the same thing really is in competition. It's not the drama that hurts the athlete so much. It's how they hold onto the drama and how long they hold onto the drama. And sometimes it's, you know, a game or two or three. The top players, they experience drama, but they get over it faster.

They reset faster. So I think that's really important. Make sure that your athletes are resetting before they continue to play after a drama. That's big. Number 17, manage your internal and external distractions. Internal distractions, of course, might be negative thoughts, self-doubt that will kind of disrupt concentration you can imagine. And external distractions like crowd noises and weather conditions and opponent's poor behavior, these are all things that can pull your athlete away from their performance goals. Performance goals are just very simple. What do they need to do right now? But some of my athletes that get distracted easily, I try to get them to play practice sets where they're keeping scored differently. So instead of 15, 30, 40, they keep scored one, two, three. And it's very simple. If you can win three points in a row, you win the game and the other dude serves. And you play out the whole set. Winning three points in a row is difficult. It requires a lot of focus. And if you've ever done like a line graph as a chart in a match where every time your athlete wins a point, you go up, when they lose a point, you go down. They win a point, you go up, and they lose, you go down. You'll see a lot of that. You'll see a lot of athletes do this and we all do it. You win a great point. It looks like you're a pro. Very next point, you give it right back. So distractions, 18 is playing to win versus playing not to lose.

That's 18 on the list. Give your athletes this little bit of an analogy that they're a Roman gladiator and they have two tools. They have a sword and a shield. Sword and a shield. Playing to win is when they use their sword, of course, and they're very confident. They're very proactive with their play. They're aggressive with their play. And playing not to lose is kind of like the shield, right? When they're more cautious and reactive. So sometimes you do want to use a shield. If the opponent maybe might be injured or they're self-destructing like crazy, and you're just going to let them self-destruct. That's fine. On big stages and on big points, I got to say the top players are the sword more often. And you've seen it the time, I know, as experienced coaches, but intermediate players, they play to win, right? They play to win until they get a big lead, they're up 5-2, and then they start to change their style of tennis. They start to play not to lose. So they almost like driving a race car. They see the finish line and they can say, okay, don't blow it. Be careful now. Just be safe. You've got to lead. And just by doing that, they've changed their whole style of tennis. And usually when you change a winning game, you're in trouble. All right, 19 is choosing avoidance or exposure. Avoidance or exposure, that's very important for us as coaches. A lot of times we would hear parents or coaches say, you can't quit, man, quitters never win.

But that's not true. Sometimes you have to quit things to improve. That would be, of course, avoidance, right? You're going to avoid doing things. So quitting sometimes for me is kind of like trimming the fat. If you could imagine eating a piece of steak, you're trimming the fat off, you're making it more lean. With our athletes, we have to trim the fat. Example might be with their stroke biomechanics, maybe their backswing is way too big and it goes back three feet too far this way, then it takes another three feet to get back to where it should be. So now it's six feet too long and the athlete hits a lot of balls in the net when their backswing is way up like this. So trimming the fat, time traveling in their mind with the distractions, like to the past or the future too much, trimming the fat, they shouldn't be thinking about those things. Trim the fat also occurs with their footwork. I'll give an example. Sometimes with athletes, this is what we see. They run to a ball wide, they hit a shot, but they take three steps to get their balance and three steps back to get back to where they should have been. That's six, right? If they do that twice a point, let's do a little bit of math just for fun. All right. So they're doing three steps three times, right? This averages out to about 130 points. Most matches are about 130 points. So when they're taking these 12 extra steps times 130 points, they're taking over 1500

extra steps in one match. Now, who's going to need an app? Who's going to be tired in the semis, the athletes that are not trimming the fat? So it's our job to do that. And the last number 20 is, it's important that you know, we know that athletes should do post-match reflections and analysis. That's very important. So post-match, let's talk about that just for a second. Here's what I hear, and you're probably here too. I call the athlete after a tournament, and I go, Van, how'd I go? How was your matches? They go, bad. And I would say, what do you mean? What happened? I lost. Yeah, but how was your performance? Didn't you hear I lost? And that's all we kind of get as coaches. But what I want you to do is ask your athletes after they emotionally decompress, ask them to do something. Write in their cell phone just three things they thought they did well, three things they want to improve, and then they're going to text these to the coaches after the tournament. And it could be a whole team of coaches. Now, that's just accountability, right? The kid does that. They're more accountable for their customized developmental plan. And as coaches, we love it. If we get the text, here's three things I did well, three things I want to improve that helps us to organize next week's plan. So I hope these 20 steps and 20 minutes that we just did, boom, hope it provided a little bit of software skills that you need, and you know they need under pressure and help

it'll help them maximize their potential at a faster rate. And thank you so much. I hope you guys enjoy the bunch of books, the book bundle you're going to be getting from tennis Australian from me as a gift and so on.
